entries.definition: Having a reduced level of alertness and a blunted response to stimulation, between drowsy and stuporous.
entries.plain: Dulled and hard to rouse, but not fully unconscious.
entries.etymology: Latin obtundere 'to beat against, blunt', from ob- (against) + tundere (to beat).
entries.exampleClinical: By the second hour he'd gone from drowsy to frankly obtunded, and we stopped waiting on the scan to protect the airway.
entries.exampleCasual: After a double night shift I'm not tired, I'm obtunded — rousable to loud coffee only.
entries.usageNote: Part of the consciousness ladder: alert → lethargic → obtunded → stuporous → comatose. Precise words beat the vague 'altered'.

entries.definition: Responsive only to vigorous or repeated, often painful, stimulation; one step short of coma.
entries.plain: Almost unrousable — only hard stimulation gets a response.
entries.etymology: Latin stupor 'numbness, dullness', from stupere (to be stunned).
entries.exampleClinical: She was stuporous to sternal rub only, which bought the neurology registrar out of bed in record time.
entries.exampleCasual: Stupor is also the everyday word for a daze — 'a drunken stupor' predates the wards by centuries.
entries.usageNote: Noun: stupor. Document what stimulus you used and what response you got — 'localizes to pain' beats 'stuporous' for handoff.

entries.definition: Drowsy and sluggish, with reduced alertness but still rousable to near-normal interaction.
entries.plain: Sleepy and slow, but you can wake them up.
entries.etymology: Greek lethargos 'forgetful, drowsy', from lethe (forgetfulness) + argos (idle).
entries.exampleClinical: The baby was feeding poorly and lethargic — in a neonate those two words together earn a full septic workup.
entries.exampleCasual: Post-lunch lectures induce a lethargy that no amount of caffeine fully reverses.
entries.usageNote: 'Somnolent' is its close twin (leaning toward sleepiness). Noun: lethargy. Milder than 'obtunded'.

entries.definition: Stiffness and resistance of the neck to passive flexion, a sign of meningeal irritation.
entries.plain: A stiff neck that resists being bent forward — a meningitis warning sign.
entries.etymology: Latin nucha 'nape of the neck' (via Arabic nukha); rigidus 'stiff'.
entries.exampleClinical: Fever, photophobia, and nuchal rigidity — start the antibiotics before the LP, not after.
entries.exampleCasual: 'Nuchal' is a quietly useful adjective; the nuchal translucency scan in pregnancy borrows the same neck.
entries.usageNote: Sits with Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs in the meningism cluster. 'Nuchal' (nape of neck) is worth knowing on its own.

entries.definition: Relating to the altered, recovering state that follows a seizure.
entries.plain: The groggy recovery period right after a seizure.
entries.etymology: Latin post- (after) + ictus (a blow, stroke).
entries.exampleClinical: He was deeply postictal in the ambulance — confused and combative — which is reassuringly typical, not a second emergency.
entries.exampleCasual: The root 'ictus' also gives us 'ictal' (during) and 'interictal' (between) — a tidy little family.
entries.usageNote: A postictal phase favors true seizure over syncope (which recovers fast). Tongue-biting and incontinence point the same way.

entries.definition: An abnormal skin sensation such as tingling, prickling, or 'pins and needles', without an external cause.
entries.plain: Tingling or pins-and-needles with no obvious trigger.
entries.etymology: Greek para- (abnormal) + aisthesis (sensation).
entries.exampleClinical: The glove-and-stocking paresthesias map a length-dependent neuropathy more clearly than any sentence could.
entries.exampleCasual: When your foot 'falls asleep', that's paresthesia — your nervous system filing a brief, confused complaint.
entries.usageNote: British spelling 'paraesthesia'. Distinguish from 'dysesthesia' (an unpleasant or painful distortion) and 'anesthesia' (absence).

entries.definition: To draw out or bring forth a sign, reflex, or piece of history through examination or questioning.
entries.plain: To bring out a sign or fact deliberately.
entries.etymology: Latin elicere 'to draw out', from e- (out) + lacere (to entice).
entries.exampleClinical: I couldn't elicit an ankle reflex even with reinforcement, which fit the rest of the neuropathy story.
entries.exampleCasual: Don't confuse it with 'illicit' (illegal) — eliciting a reflex is very much above board.
entries.usageNote: High-frequency exam verb. The sound-alike 'illicit' is an adjective; see the Mix-ups tab for the trap.

entries.definition: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably; unstable.
entries.plain: Swinging up and down unpredictably.
entries.etymology: Latin labilis 'apt to slip', from labi (to slide, fall).
entries.exampleClinical: Her sugars are labile on the current regimen — sixteen one hour, four the next — so we're switching strategy entirely.
entries.exampleCasual: After the news the whole ward team was emotionally labile; even the consultant's voice wobbled.
entries.usageNote: Most US clinicians say LAY-bile. Spans endocrine (sugars, BP), psychiatry (mood), and chemistry (a labile compound).

entries.definition: Not responding to standard treatment; resistant to attempts at management.
entries.plain: Not budging despite the usual treatment.
entries.etymology: Latin refractarius 'stubborn', from refringere (to break up).
entries.exampleClinical: The seizures were refractory to two agents at full dose, so the conversation turned to the ICU and an infusion.
entries.exampleCasual: My houseplant is refractory to every watering schedule known to science.
entries.usageNote: Takes 'to': refractory to therapy. Escalation ladder of stubbornness: resistant → refractory → recalcitrant.

entries.definition: Easily crumbled or torn, and prone to bleed on minimal contact.
entries.plain: So fragile it crumbles or bleeds at the lightest touch.
entries.etymology: Latin friabilis 'easily crumbled', from friare (to rub away).
collocations: bled when friable tissue was touched
entries.exampleClinical: The tumor was so friable that it bled at the lightest brush of the scope — biopsy was almost an afterthought.
entries.exampleCasual: Friable is the perfect word for an over-baked cookie, though pathologists rarely use it that way.
entries.usageNote: Pronounced FRY-able. Endoscopy and surgery reports lean on it heavily; it implies 'bleeds easily' as much as 'crumbly'.

entries.definition: Abnormally hardened, especially of skin or soft tissue.
entries.plain: Hardened and firm to the touch.
entries.etymology: Latin indurare 'to harden', from in- (intensive) + durus (hard).
entries.exampleClinical: We read the TB test by the induration, not the redness — a finger over the forearm tells you more than the eye.
entries.exampleCasual: Induration is what you feel; erythema is what you see — a useful split when describing any angry patch of skin.
entries.usageNote: Noun: induration. The Mantoux/TST is measured by induration diameter in millimeters, never by redness.

entries.definition: Of a malignant tumor, to spread from its primary site to distant parts of the body.
entries.plain: To spread to other parts of the body.
entries.etymology: Greek metastasis 'a removal, change', from meta- (change) + histanai (to place).
entries.exampleClinical: Staging showed it had already metastasized to bone, which redrew the whole plan around comfort and control.
entries.exampleCasual: People borrow it figuratively — 'the argument metastasized into a family feud' — and it always sounds ominous.
entries.usageNote: Noun: metastasis (plural metastases /-siːz/); spoken shorthand 'mets'. Adjective: metastatic. 'Metastatic burden' = how much tumor is out there.

entries.definition: Pinpoint, non-blanching red or purple spots caused by tiny capillary hemorrhages into the skin.
entries.plain: Tiny pinpoint spots of bleeding under the skin.
entries.etymology: Italian petecchia 'a small spot'.
entries.exampleClinical: Non-blanching petechiae over the shins in a feverish child — press a glass to them and don't relax if they stay.
entries.exampleCasual: The bleeding-into-skin ladder by size: petechiae (pinpoint), purpura (patches), ecchymoses (bruises).
entries.usageNote: Plural; singular 'petechia'. Adjective: petechial. The defining test is non-blanching — they don't fade under pressure.

entries.definition: A larger area of bleeding under the skin — a bruise — from rupture of subcutaneous vessels.
entries.plain: A bruise; a flat patch of bleeding under the skin.
entries.etymology: Greek ekchymosis, from ek- (out) + chymos (juice).
entries.exampleClinical: Spontaneous ecchymoses in unusual places sent us straight to a coagulation screen.
entries.exampleCasual: When you want to make a simple bruise sound serious in a presentation, reach for 'ecchymosis'.
entries.usageNote: Plural ecchymoses /-siːz/. The three-rung ladder petechiae < purpura < ecchymoses is worth memorizing by size.

entries.definition: To transfer blood or a blood product into a patient's circulation.
entries.plain: To give a patient blood through a drip.
entries.etymology: Latin transfundere 'to pour across', from trans- (across) + fundere (to pour).
entries.exampleClinical: His hemoglobin hit sixty-five with ongoing bleeding, so we crossmatched and transfused two units without much debate.
entries.exampleCasual: On call you'll say 'let's transfuse him' more times than you'll say your own name.
entries.usageNote: Noun: transfusion. Said in 'units'. 'Crossmatch' (verify compatibility) is the verb that should precede it whenever time allows.

entries.definition: Of a pathogen, highly capable of causing severe disease; extremely harmful in its effects.
entries.plain: A germ that's especially good at making you very sick.
entries.etymology: Latin virulentus 'full of poison', from virus (poison).
entries.exampleClinical: This was a particularly virulent strain — healthy adults were in the ICU within a day of their first symptom.
entries.exampleCasual: It crosses over nicely: 'virulent criticism' is the verbal version of a nasty pathogen.
entries.usageNote: Noun: virulence. 'Virulence factors' are the molecular tools that make a microbe dangerous; the vaccine word 'attenuated' is its opposite.

entries.definition: Of a microorganism, having complex nutritional requirements that make it difficult to culture.
entries.plain: A germ that's fussy and hard to grow in the lab.
entries.etymology: Latin fastidiosus 'disdainful, particular', from fastidium (loathing).
entries.exampleClinical: HACEK organisms are fastidious, so warn the lab to hold the cultures longer or you'll chase a false negative.
entries.exampleCasual: Same word, human version: a fastidious eater sends back the soup three times. The microbes are no less particular.
entries.usageNote: In micro, a near-technical sense ('hard to grow'); in general English it means meticulously fussy. The lab meaning surprises learners.

entries.definition: Originating in or acquired within a hospital; of an infection, hospital-acquired.
entries.plain: Picked up in the hospital itself.
entries.etymology: Greek nosokomeion 'hospital', from nosos (disease) + komein (to care for).
entries.exampleClinical: Pneumonia appearing on day five points to a nosocomial organism, so the empiric cover broadens accordingly.
entries.exampleCasual: The plainer 'hospital-acquired' is winning the usage war, but 'nosocomial' still earns its place in exams.
entries.usageNote: The community-acquired vs nosocomial split drives empiric antibiotic choice. 'Iatrogenic' (caused by treatment) is a related but distinct idea.

entries.definition: Caused inadvertently by medical examination, treatment, or advice.
entries.plain: A problem the medical care itself caused.
entries.etymology: Greek iatros (physician) + -genic (producing).
entries.exampleClinical: The pneumothorax was iatrogenic — a known risk of the central line, disclosed and now being managed.
entries.exampleCasual: It's the honest word for 'we caused this', which is exactly why it matters that the word exists.
entries.usageNote: From iatros, physician (also in 'psychiatry', 'pediatric'). Naming iatrogenic harm plainly is part of good clinical culture.

entries.definition: Of treatment, started on the basis of clinical judgement and probability before definitive test results are available.
entries.plain: Treating on best-guess grounds before the tests confirm it.
entries.etymology: Greek empeirikos 'experienced', from en- (in) + peira (trial).
entries.exampleClinical: We started empiric broad-spectrum cover at the door and narrowed it once the cultures spoke two days later.
entries.exampleCasual: Adverb 'empirically' has a second life in research, meaning 'shown by actual data' rather than theory.
entries.usageNote: The arc is empiric → de-escalate → targeted. 'Empirical' (data-driven) is the same word wearing its scientific hat.

entries.definition: Intended to prevent disease rather than treat it once present.
entries.plain: Given to prevent a problem before it starts.
entries.etymology: Greek prophylaktikos 'guarding against', from pro- (before) + phylassein (to guard).
entries.exampleClinical: Everyone immobile on this ward gets prophylactic anticoagulation unless there's a bleeding reason not to.
entries.exampleCasual: Noun: prophylaxis. 'DVT prophylaxis' is muttered on every ward round like a small daily prayer.
entries.usageNote: Prophylactic dose (preventive) is usually lower than treatment dose — a distinction with real consequences for anticoagulants.

entries.definition: To adjust the dose of a drug incrementally against a measured response or target.
entries.plain: To fine-tune a drug dose up or down until it hits the target.
entries.etymology: French titre 'proportion, standard', from medieval Latin titulus.
collocations: titrate the infusion against blood pressure
entries.exampleClinical: Titrate the noradrenaline to a MAP of sixty-five and let the number, not the habit, set the rate.
entries.exampleCasual: I titrate my caffeine to lecture difficulty — a slow morning infusion, a bolus before statistics.
entries.usageNote: The signature phrase is 'titrate to effect'. Borrowed from chemistry's titration; the medical sense is now everywhere in the ICU.

entries.definition: To reduce a drug dose gradually in steps, usually to avoid withdrawal or rebound.
entries.plain: To step a medication down slowly rather than stopping suddenly.
entries.etymology: From 'taper', a thin candle that narrows to a point.
collocations: taper the dose over two weeks
entries.exampleClinical: After three weeks of prednisone you can't just stop — write a taper, or the adrenal axis will protest.
entries.exampleCasual: I'm on a slow taper off late-night studying; the withdrawal symptoms are surprisingly real.
entries.usageNote: Noun and verb both used: 'a steroid taper', 'taper the dose'. Overlaps with 'wean'; 'taper' is the drug-specific choice.

entries.definition: Inadvisable or unsafe to use in a particular situation because of the harm it could cause.
entries.plain: A treatment you must not use here because it would do harm.
entries.etymology: Latin contra- (against) + indicare (to point out).
entries.exampleClinical: Beta-blockers are contraindicated in his cocaine-driven chest pain — the textbook trap, set and waiting.
entries.exampleCasual: Noun: contraindication. The mirror word 'indicated' (this is the right thing to use) completes the pair.
entries.usageNote: Absolute (never) vs relative (weigh the risk) contraindication is a distinction examiners adore. Opposite: 'indicated'.

entries.definition: To increase the effect or potency of another agent, often more than additively.
entries.plain: To make another drug's effect stronger.
entries.etymology: Latin potentia 'power', from posse (to be able).
entries.exampleClinical: Warn him that alcohol potentiates the sedative — the combination does more than the sum of the labels.
entries.exampleCasual: Good sleep potentiates everything else you do; it's the quiet co-factor of a productive week.
entries.usageNote: Close to 'synergistic' (two agents together exceed the sum). 'Potentiate' usually means one agent boosting another.

entries.definition: Fluctuating in intensity, with periods of worsening and improvement over time.
entries.plain: Coming and going in waves — better, then worse, then better.
entries.etymology: From the phases of the moon: waxing (growing) and waning (shrinking).
entries.exampleClinical: His confusion waxes and wanes through the day, which is delirium's signature far more than dementia's.
entries.exampleCasual: My motivation for the thesis waxes and wanes with roughly lunar regularity.
entries.usageNote: A lovely lunar metaphor that survives in clinical English. The fluctuating-attention sense is near-diagnostic for delirium.

entries.definition: Of an illness, resolving on its own within a predictable time without specific treatment.
entries.plain: Gets better by itself without treatment.
entries.etymology: From 'self' + Latin limes (boundary, limit).
entries.exampleClinical: Reassure them it's a self-limited viral illness, give the safety-net advice, and resist the urge to prescribe.
entries.exampleCasual: Most of my Sunday existential crises are self-limited — gone by Monday's first coffee.
entries.usageNote: Also written 'self-limiting'. The cornerstone phrase for explaining why a virus needs patience, not antibiotics.

entries.definition: Difficult to manage, alleviate, or cure despite vigorous effort.
entries.plain: Stubbornly resistant to any attempt to control it.
entries.etymology: Latin intractabilis 'unmanageable', from in- (not) + tractare (to handle).
entries.exampleClinical: Her intractable nausea defeated three antiemetics, so palliative care joined to think laterally.
entries.exampleCasual: Outside medicine: an intractable problem, an intractable bureaucracy — the flavor of immovable difficulty carries over.
entries.usageNote: Overlaps with 'refractory' but feels more emphatic and is used freely outside medicine too.

entries.definition: Of a prognosis, uncertain with a real risk of poor outcome; cautiously pessimistic.
entries.plain: An uncertain outlook that could still go badly.
entries.etymology: From 'guard' — a guarded statement holds something back.
entries.exampleClinical: We told the family the prognosis was guarded — honest about the uncertainty without slamming the door on hope.
entries.exampleCasual: Don't confuse it with 'grave', which is far darker; guarded leaves the window open a crack.
entries.usageNote: Prognosis register, mildest to darkest: favorable → guarded → poor → grave → dismal. Pick the rung deliberately.

entries.definition: To die from the effects of a disease or injury; to finally yield to an overpowering force.
entries.plain: To die from an illness, in gentler words.
entries.etymology: Latin succumbere 'to lie down under', from sub- (under) + cumbere (to lie).
entries.exampleClinical: Despite everything the team threw at it, he succumbed to the sepsis on the fourth night.
entries.exampleCasual: Lighter uses survive too: 'I finally succumbed to the dessert menu' — yielding, not dying.
entries.usageNote: A softened, dignified way to write of death in case summaries. Takes 'to': succumb to the disease.

entries.definition: Showing no abnormal or noteworthy findings; normal.
entries.plain: Nothing abnormal worth noting.
entries.etymology: From 'remarkable' (worth remarking on) + negating 'un-'.
entries.exampleClinical: Abdomen soft, chest clear, neuro intact — the exam was reassuringly unremarkable.
entries.exampleCasual: It's the highest praise a radiologist offers: an unremarkable scan is a small celebration.
entries.usageNote: The standard charting word for 'normal, and I did look'. 'Otherwise unremarkable' tidily closes a section after one finding.

entries.definition: On overall or naked-eye assessment, without fine or detailed testing.
entries.plain: On the rough, big-picture look — no fine testing done.
entries.etymology: Latin grossus 'thick, coarse'.
entries.exampleClinical: Cranial nerves grossly intact — meaning a screening look, not the slow forty-step exam, was reassuring.
entries.exampleCasual: Don't read 'grossly' as 'disgustingly'; here it just means 'on the whole'.
entries.usageNote: 'Grossly intact' flags a screening-level exam and quietly hedges that subtle deficits weren't formally excluded. Also: gross anatomy, gross specimen.

entries.definition: Showing cachexia — profound wasting of muscle and fat from chronic illness.
entries.plain: Severely wasted and thin from long illness.
entries.etymology: Greek kakos (bad) + hexis (condition).
entries.exampleClinical: He looked cachectic from the doorway — the kind of wasting that tells half the story before the notes do.
entries.exampleCasual: The opening line of a case often hinges on appearance: well-nourished, cachectic, or toxic-appearing.
entries.usageNote: Noun: cachexia /kəˈkɛksiə/. A weighty word — reserve it for genuine wasting, not ordinary thinness.

entries.definition: Looking acutely and severely unwell — flushed, listless, and obviously sick at first glance.
entries.plain: Looking really, obviously sick the moment you see them.
entries.etymology: Greek toxikon 'poison for arrows' + 'appearing'.
entries.exampleClinical: The vitals were borderline, but she was toxic-appearing — and the gestalt outranked the numbers that night.
entries.exampleCasual: Pediatricians live by the well-appearing versus toxic-appearing split; it triages before a single test returns.
entries.usageNote: Encodes clinical gestalt in one hyphenated word. 'Well-appearing' is the reassuring opposite that reviewers look for.

entries.definition: To follow a measured value over time by repeating the test to see its direction.
entries.plain: To repeat a test over time and watch which way it's heading.
entries.etymology: Old English trendan 'to roll, turn'.
entries.exampleClinical: One lactate means little — trend it, and the slope tells you whether the resuscitation is working.
entries.exampleCasual: The whole ward speaks in slopes: 'his creatinine is trending down' is genuine good news.
entries.usageNote: A clinical verb built from a noun. 'Serial' is its adjective cousin: serial troponins, serial abdominal exams.

entries.definition: Of a result, falsely abnormal because of a technical or sampling artifact rather than true physiology.
entries.plain: A fake-looking result caused by a lab or sampling glitch.
entries.etymology: Latin spurius 'illegitimate, false'.
entries.exampleClinical: The potassium of seven didn't fit a well patient with a normal ECG — spurious hemolysis, confirmed on the repeat.
entries.exampleCasual: It generalizes neatly: a spurious correlation in the data is one that doesn't actually mean anything.
entries.usageNote: Near-synonym 'artifactual'. 'Spurious hyperkalemia' (pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis) is the canonical example.

entries.definition: Suggestive of a specified serious diagnosis and warranting further evaluation.
entries.plain: Pointing worryingly toward a particular diagnosis.
entries.etymology: From 'concern', Latin concernere (to relate to, sift together).
entries.exampleClinical: The CT described a mass concerning for malignancy, which set the staging machinery in motion before lunch.
entries.exampleCasual: American clinical English loves these hedged-but-pointed phrases — concerning for, suspicious for, consistent with.
entries.usageNote: Part of the calibrated reporting ladder: consistent with (fits) < suspicious for < concerning for < diagnostic of. Note 'for', not 'of'.

entries.definition: Compatible with a given diagnosis, though not proving it exclusively.
entries.plain: Fits the diagnosis, without proving it on its own.
entries.etymology: Latin consistere 'to stand firm together'.
entries.exampleClinical: The film was consistent with pneumonia, but I chose my words so nobody would read it as proof.
entries.exampleCasual: It's the careful scientist's favorite hedge — the data are 'consistent with' the hypothesis, never quite 'proof of' it.
entries.usageNote: The softest rung of diagnostic certainty — compatible, not confirmatory. British reports prefer 'in keeping with'.

entries.definition: Of a gait, adopted to avoid pain, typically by shortening time spent bearing weight on the painful side.
entries.plain: A limping walk that protects a painful leg.
entries.etymology: Greek anti- (against) + algos (pain).
entries.exampleClinical: He came in with a clearly antalgic gait, shifting his weight off the right hip almost before he reached the chair.
entries.exampleCasual: Watching how a patient walks from the waiting room is free diagnostic data — antalgic, ataxic, or shuffling all show.
entries.usageNote: From the same anti-pain root as 'analgesic'. Gait adjectives — antalgic, ataxic, shuffling, spastic — each name a mechanism.

entries.definition: Showing a lack of voluntary coordination of muscle movements, typically a broad-based unsteady gait.
entries.plain: Uncoordinated and unsteady on the feet.
entries.etymology: Greek a- (without) + taxis (order, arrangement).
entries.exampleClinical: Her broad-based, ataxic gait pointed the workup squarely at the cerebellum.
entries.exampleCasual: The literal root is 'without order' — a satisfyingly honest description of bumping into the furniture.
entries.usageNote: Noun: ataxia. Localizes toward the cerebellum or proprioceptive pathways. Don't confuse with the pain-driven 'antalgic' gait.

entries.definition: A period during which the signs and symptoms of a disease abate, partially or completely.
entries.plain: A stretch where the disease quiets down or disappears.
entries.etymology: Latin remittere 'to send back, slacken'.
entries.exampleClinical: The marrow came back clean — complete remission — and you could feel the whole room exhale.
entries.exampleCasual: Outside oncology people borrow it hopefully: 'my procrastination is in remission this week'.
entries.usageNote: The triad remission / relapse / refractory organizes oncology and chronic inflammatory disease alike. 'Cure' is a bolder word, used cautiously.

entries.definition: The return of disease activity after a period of improvement or remission.
entries.plain: The illness coming back after it had eased.
entries.etymology: Latin relabi 'to slip back', from re- (back) + labi (to slide).
entries.exampleClinical: An early relapse like this, only months after remission, usually signals a more aggressive biology.
entries.exampleCasual: It crosses into addiction and habit talk constantly — 'relapse' is a heavy, human word.
entries.usageNote: Verb and noun both: 'she relapsed'. 'Relapsing-remitting' is the defining course pattern for multiple sclerosis.

entries.definition: An abnormal accumulation of fluid within a body cavity or joint space.
entries.plain: Fluid that has pooled inside a joint or body cavity.
entries.etymology: Latin effundere 'to pour out', from ex- (out) + fundere (to pour).
entries.exampleClinical: The knee held a tense effusion, so we aspirated it both to settle it and to send the fluid for answers.
entries.exampleCasual: Same root as 'effusive' — a person overflowing with praise is, etymologically, just leaking enthusiasm.
entries.usageNote: Location names the problem: pleural, pericardial, joint. 'Tap' or 'aspirate' is the verb for sampling it.

entries.definition: A grating or crackling sensation felt or heard, from bone ends, roughened joint surfaces, or gas in tissue.
entries.plain: A grinding or crackling you feel under the skin or in a joint.
entries.etymology: Latin crepitus 'a rattling, creaking', from crepare (to crackle).
entries.exampleClinical: Crackling crepitus under the skin of the chest wall meant air where air should never be — surgical emphysema.
entries.exampleCasual: My knees produce a recreational crepitus on every staircase; the orthopods assure me it's mostly benign.
entries.usageNote: Subcutaneous crepitus (palpable gas) is the alarming kind. Joint crepitus is often harmless. Same word, very different stakes.

entries.definition: Itchy; causing or characterized by the urge to scratch.
entries.plain: Itchy.
entries.etymology: Latin prurire 'to itch'.
entries.exampleClinical: The rash was intensely pruritic and worse at night, which nudged scabies toward the top of the list.
entries.exampleCasual: 'Pruritic' is simply the dignified, three-syllable way to say a rash itches like mad.
entries.usageNote: Noun: pruritus /prʊˈraɪtəs/ — note the pronunciation shifts. Generalized pruritus without a rash can flag systemic disease.

entries.definition: Shedding or peeling of the outer layers of the skin.
entries.plain: Skin peeling off in flakes or sheets.
entries.etymology: Latin desquamare 'to scale off', from de- (off) + squama (scale).
entries.exampleClinical: Days after the fever broke, the palms began a sheet-like desquamation that handed us the diagnosis retrospectively.
entries.exampleCasual: A bad sunburn ends in desquamation; you've shed skin like a scaly creature, medically speaking.
entries.usageNote: From squama, 'scale'. Sheet-like vs fine desquamation, and its timing after a rash, can be a diagnostic clue (Kawasaki, scarlet fever).

entries.definition: Having a normal volume of body fluid — neither dehydrated nor overloaded.
entries.plain: Just-right on body fluid — not dry, not overloaded.
entries.etymology: Greek eu- (good, normal) + Latin volumen (volume) + Greek haima (blood).
entries.exampleClinical: Classifying the hyponatremia starts at the bedside: is she hypovolemic, euvolemic, or overloaded? Euvolemic points at SIADH.
entries.exampleCasual: The 'eu-' prefix is a gift — euvolemic, euthyroid, euthymic all just mean 'the good, normal version'.
entries.usageNote: The 'eu-' (normal) family is worth collecting: euthyroid, euvolemic, eupneic. Volume status is the first fork in the hyponatremia algorithm.

entries.definition: Having normal thyroid function.
entries.plain: Thyroid working normally.
entries.etymology: Greek eu- (normal) + thyreoeides (shield-shaped, the thyroid).
entries.exampleClinical: She's euthyroid on her current levothyroxine dose, so we'll leave well alone and recheck in a year.
entries.exampleCasual: Once you spot the 'eu-' pattern, half of endocrinology vocabulary stops being intimidating.
entries.usageNote: 'Euthyroid sick syndrome' confusingly describes abnormal thyroid labs in a non-thyroidal illness — the exception that tests the rule.

entries.definition: Having viable bacteria circulating in the bloodstream.
entries.plain: Having bacteria in the blood.
entries.etymology: Greek bakterion (small rod) + haima (blood).
entries.exampleClinical: If he stays bacteremic on appropriate antibiotics, hunt for the source — an abscess or a seeded valve isn't clearing itself.
entries.exampleCasual: Noun: bacteremia. The mental jump from 'bacteremic' to 'where's the source?' is a habit worth building early.
entries.usageNote: Persistent bacteremia despite therapy is a red flag for endocarditis or undrained collections. Compare 'septic' (the host response).

entries.definition: Of a device, left in place within the body for an extended period.
entries.plain: A tube or line left inside the body for a while.
entries.etymology: From 'in' + 'dwell' (to remain, reside).
entries.exampleClinical: Any indwelling line is a suspect in a new fever — the catheter you forgot about is the one that's seeding the blood.
entries.exampleCasual: It's a quietly elegant word: the device 'dwells within', like an unwelcome long-term houseguest.
entries.usageNote: Indwelling devices are classic infection sources ('line sepsis'). 'Source control' often just means removing the indwelling culprit.

entries.definition: Abnormal protrusion of one or both eyeballs, classically from Graves' disease.
entries.plain: Bulging eyes, classically from an overactive thyroid.
entries.etymology: Greek ex- (out) + ophthalmos (eye).
entries.exampleClinical: The exophthalmos and lid lag told the story before the TSH came back flat.
entries.exampleCasual: Spelling it is its own exam — that silent 'ph' cluster trips up nearly everyone.
entries.usageNote: Near-synonym 'proptosis' is used more broadly (any cause); 'exophthalmos' leans thyroid. Note the tricky 'xophth' cluster.

entries.definition: To narrow or step down therapy, especially antibiotics, once culture results allow more targeted treatment.
entries.plain: To switch from broad, just-in-case treatment to a narrower targeted one.
entries.etymology: From 'escalate' (Latin scala, ladder) with reversing 'de-'.
entries.exampleClinical: Cultures grew a sensitive organism, so we de-escalated from the carbapenem to plain amoxicillin and slept easier about resistance.
entries.exampleCasual: The word travels well: de-escalating a tense conversation uses the same downward-step logic.
entries.usageNote: Core antibiotic-stewardship verb. The arc empiric → de-escalate → targeted is worth saying aloud until it's automatic.

entries.definition: At the point of death; in a critical, rapidly deteriorating state.
entries.plain: On the very edge of death.
entries.etymology: Latin in extremis 'in the furthest reaches' (of life).
entries.exampleClinical: He rolled through the doors in extremis — there was time to act, not to deliberate.
entries.exampleCasual: It keeps its Latin dignity, used half-seriously even outside medicine: 'I submitted the essay in extremis, two minutes to midnight'.
entries.usageNote: Untranslated Latin, kept for gravity. 'Moribund' is the near-synonym for a patient slowly, inevitably dying.

entries.definition: A mass or lesion discovered by chance on imaging performed for an unrelated reason.
entries.plain: A lump found by accident on a scan done for something else.
entries.etymology: English 'incidental' + the tumor suffix -oma — a playful modern coinage.
entries.exampleClinical: The CT cleared the appendix but turned up an adrenal incidentaloma, and now we owe him a conversation and a plan.
entries.exampleCasual: It's a knowingly tongue-in-cheek word — doctors invented '-oma' for 'oops, found a thing' and somehow it stuck.
entries.usageNote: A modern, semi-jocular coinage now firmly in use. The plainer 'incidental finding' is the formal alternative in reports.

entries.definition: Abnormal sensitivity to and discomfort from light.
entries.plain: Light hurts the eyes.
entries.etymology: Greek phos, photos (light) + phobos (fear).
entries.exampleClinical: Headache, fever, photophobia, and a stiff neck cluster into one urgent question you have to answer fast.
entries.exampleCasual: After a migraine, ordinary daylight feels like an interrogation lamp — textbook photophobia.
entries.usageNote: Here '-phobia' means physical intolerance, not psychological fear. Adjective: photophobic. Travels with meningism and migraine.
